abstract.t: This internal working draft divides cluster routing into eight high-level problem areas. It defines their scope and expected design outcomes without selecting a cluster architecture.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: PulseBeam needs a way to locate resources and deliver packets between participants connected to different nodes. This document identifies the problems that a cluster routing design needs to address and provides boundaries for designing them separately.

This is a proposed scope for further design, not a description of implemented behavior or an IETF submission. It does not select a topology, routing algorithm, consistency model, protocol, or set of node roles. It defines no wire protocol and changes no compatibility contract.

section.name: Cluster Membership
section.t: Which nodes exist and are available? Define node identity, capabilities, availability, and the membership-view contract.

section.name: Resource Placement and Ownership
section.t: Where do participants and publications reside, and who is authoritative for them? Define placement and ownership semantics, including changes of ownership.

section.name: Resource Discovery
section.t: How are participants and publications located? Define the semantics for resolving, enumerating, and watching resources.

section.name: Subscription Management
section.t: How is receiver demand tracked and propagated? Define the subscription lifecycle and representation of demand.

section.name: Route Computation
section.t: How are packet-forwarding paths selected? Define routing inputs, constraints, and the contract for expressing forwarding paths.

section.name: Route Execution
section.t: How are forwarding paths installed and packets forwarded? Define local forwarding state and the contract for updating it.

section.name: Inter-Node Transport
section.t: How do nodes communicate and exchange packets? Define the contracts for peer communication and packet transfer.

section.name: Failure Recovery
section.t: How are failures detected and correct routing restored? Define failure detection, reconciliation, and recovery semantics across the affected areas.

section.name: Design Boundaries
section.t: Each area needs a design contract describing its inputs, outputs, invariants, failure semantics, and dependencies. Decisions in one area should not unnecessarily prescribe implementation choices in another.

These areas are logically separable, but they interact at runtime. Their interfaces and shared invariants need to be reconciled. This decomposition does not require separate services, crates, processes, or RFCs.
Security, admission, scalability, observability, and performance are cross-cutting concerns to evaluate across the areas. No particular allocation of these responsibilities is implied.

ol.li: Each area has an explicit design contract and defined boundaries.
Dependencies and shared invariants are documented.
Alternative designs can be evaluated without assuming a preferred cluster topology.
The resulting architecture has no unresolved ownership gaps or conflicting responsibilities.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Cluster design affects who can join, advertise resources, request subscriptions, install routes, and receive traffic. Incorrect or conflicting authority across these boundaries can enable unauthorized disclosure, misrouting, or denial of service. The designs for the individual areas need to define their trust assumptions, authorization boundaries, and resource limits together; this document selects no security mechanism.

section.name: Open Questions
section.t: The design of each problem area and the contracts between them remain open. Existing proposals are candidates for evaluation, not decisions imposed by this document.
